extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: A GDPR-compliant French speech dataset containing simultaneous recordings from five body-conduction audio sensors and an airborne reference microphone. The publicly released corpus contains 45.62 hours per sensor from 188 participants, organized into speech-clean, speech-noisy, speechless-clean, and speechless-noisy subsets, with recording-condition annotations, textual transcripts, and phonetic transcripts.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Éric Bavu
extraction.citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A controlled recording protocol was conducted with 200 participants, of whom 188 were retained after post-processing. A Zoom F8n recorded six sensors simultaneously at 48 kHz with 32-bit resolution: an airborne headset microphone, a forehead accelerometer, soft and rigid in-ear microphones, a throat microphone, and a temple vibration pickup. Each participant completed four consecutive stages: reading French Wikipedia sentences for 15 minutes in quiet conditions; remaining silent while moving, swallowing, and breathing naturally for 2 minutes 24 seconds during spatialized ambient noise; remaining silent for 54 seconds in quiet conditions; and reading sentences for 54 seconds during spatialized noise. Noise was rendered through a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers. Recordings were monitored and validated during collection, and dedicated front-end and back-end recording software was developed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The speech-noisy subset lacks a clean reference signal. Some initially collected clips had inconsistencies caused by mispronunciation, sensor movement, occasional sensor malfunction, or a microphone inadvertently being left unequipped.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio was recorded directly from participants wearing six audio sensors. Reading prompts originated from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. A significant proportion of ambient noise excerpts came from AudioSet, particularly classes relevant to battlefield and industrial environments. Additional noise came from in-house third- and fifth-order ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For experimental training in noisy conditions while preserving a clean reference, speechless-noisy recordings were dynamically mixed with speech-clean recordings. Speaker-verification experiments used a static mixture of those subsets to preserve identical test pairs across quiet and noisy conditions. Speech-enhancement training resampled signals to 16 kHz and used Torchaudio speed perturbation, pitch shifting, and time masking as data augmentation. These procedures are described for the experiments, rather than as replacements for the released raw recordings.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was applied uniformly to all acquisition channels. Reading prompts were filtered to exclude most proper names except common first names, French town or region names, and country names; sentences containing numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors were removed. Text was lowercased and punctuation removed except apostrophes. Speech-clean recordings were automatically filtered using phoneme error rate and sensor-level speech/silence energy indicators. Retained samples had to satisfy the pronunciation criterion around a 10% phoneme error rate threshold, an SNR greater than 1.5 dB for each sensor, and speech levels exceeding each sensor's mean silence level. The other three subsets were retained only for participants with a nonempty filtered speech-clean subset. Filtering retained 188 of 200 participants and 28,471 sentences. Voice-activity timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on each side; when adjusted timestamps exceeded recording boundaries, 15 ms was trimmed on the affected side. Speakers were assigned to 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test splits separately for male and female speakers, with no speaker overlap and consistent assignments across subsets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each read utterance generated a separate recording, and its source-text transcription was retained. Recording-condition annotations are included. Normalized text was converted into International Phonetic Alphabet transcriptions covering 33 French phonemes using the CoML lab's text phonemizer. Words that triggered unwanted language switches or were unrecognized by the phonemizer were manually transcribed phonetically.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Label quality was checked by computing the Levenshtein-based phoneme error rate between the labeled phonetic transcription and a phonemized Whisper transcription. Recordings with phoneme error rates above 10% were discarded to address discrepancies between the retained text and actual pronunciation. The paper notes that French liaison is absent from the labeled phonetic transcription and caused frequent insertion or omission errors in evaluated models; liaison-related errors were excluded from the reported analysis of in-word phonetic confusions.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab Phonemizer for text-to-phoneme transcription; whisper-timestamped, based on Whisper and dynamic time warping, for transcription alignment, word timestamps, voiced-segment identification, and label-quality filtering.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset citation identifies revision 071945b. No update schedule, maintainer responsibilities, or deprecation policy is stated.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes voice recordings and physiological sounds, including breathing and sounds relevant to heart-rate tracking. Speaker gender and age are reported: 97 female and 91 male participants, with ages ranging from 18 to 82 years, an overall mean age of 28.55 years, and a median age of 25 years. The recorded speech language is French. The paper states that informed consent was obtained and that data were anonymized and encrypted during storage and analysis.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors aim to support robust communication in noisy environments, including military and industrial applications. Discussed applications include voice commands, biometric authentication and access control, identifying known voices in intercepted transmissions, and monitoring physiological signals. The paper also discusses potential battlefield-forensics uses of biometric information for tracking life signals and revealing emotional states. Ethical considerations emphasize GDPR compliance, informed consent, communicating the collection purpose, anonymization, encryption, copyright compliance for Wikipedia text, and recruiting a diverse, gender-balanced participant group.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset lacks a clean reference and cannot directly support the paired-reference speech-enhancement training used in the paper. Automatic quality filters did not detect every defect, including inadequate acoustic sealing when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone. Insertion and sealing defects affected both in-ear microphone types and degraded performance in noise. Body-conduction recordings have sensor-dependent bandwidth limitations, self-noise, and substantial participant-dependent bandwidth variability. Filtering excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences, prioritizing rigorous sensor comparisons over maximizing overall performance. French liaison is not represented in the labeled phonetic transcriptions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, testing, and fine-tuning for speech enhancement, bandwidth extension, speech recognition, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. Simultaneous sensor recordings support comparative sensor and signal-processing analyses. Speech-clean supplies paired body-conduction and airborne reference speech; speechless-noisy can be mixed with speech-clean to train noise-robust models while preserving a clean target. Speech-noisy provides real noisy-condition evaluation and phonetic labels for recognition training, but lacks a clean reference for paired-reference enhancement training. Speechless-clean supports physiological and sensor-noise analysis, heart-rate tracking, and synthetic data generation with realistic physiological noise. Additional proposed applications include voice commands and robust communication systems.
